events.title: Poetry Group
events.description:
Writing poetry is a solitary endeavor. Are you looking for feedback on your poems? You are invited to join the Poetry Group at NWPL for sharing and critique. We meet weekly on Mondays 4 pm for about an hour and a half.*

What does it mean to critique something? According to the Oxford Dictionary, “noun: critique: a detailed analysis and assessment of something, especially a literary, philosophical, or political theory.”

Since “critique” has negative connotations, we operate in workshop format. How? Billy Collins suggested “5 Things to Consider When Analyzing Poetry in an online ‘MasterClass.’”

“Poetry involves different elements like language, rhythm, and structure. Together, they tell a story and create a complexity that is unique to poetic verse. When studying poems in-depth, look at these individual elements:

  • Theme: Poetry often conveys a message through figurative language. The central idea and the subject matter can reveal the underlying theme of a poem.
  • Language: From word choice to imagery, language creates the mood and tone of a poem. The way language is arranged also impacts the rhythm of a poem.
  • Sound and rhythm: The syllabic patterns and stresses create the metrical pattern of a poem.
  • Structure: The framework of a poem’s structure affects how it is meant to be read. A poet sculpts their story around stanzas, line breaks, rhyme patterns, punctuation, and pauses.
  • Context: The who, what, where, when, and why of a poem can help explain its purpose. Look at these elements to discover the context of a poem.”

This group is open to all; RSVP is appreciated. Please email [contact omitted].

* Any changes to the schedule will be noted on the website calendar.

events.title: Read, Cook, Eat! | Cookbook Club
events.description:
Do you like to read about cooking, experiment with recipes, share stories about food with others, and eat good food? If so, we invite you to join Read, Cook, Eat!, a cookbook discussion group. We meet at the library monthly on the 3rd Tuesday at 6 pm to share our creations.*

Newcomers are always welcome; you don’t need kitchen credentials to join! Please email [contact omitted] to register – not required but it helps us figure out how to set up the tables and chairs. And we’ll keep you updated on the books selected, or visit the Book Discussion Group page for current and past book or topic selections.

Important Details

  • Cookbooks & Recipes – We will hold a copy of the cookbook at the circulation desk for you to browse and pick out recipes you might wish to try. We’ll copy them at no charge (or you can take a photo with your phone). A second copy of the cookbook will be available to borrow for 3 days during the month leading up to the meeting.
  • Quantity & Balance – This is a true potluck affair! There may be 3 desserts and 4 vegetable dishes or an appetizer and 5 different main dishes… Since recipe yields vary widely, there is no set amount of food to bring. The goal is to discover new combinations of ingredients and flavors.
  • Equipment & Utensils – While the library has a microwave and stove for reheating, the kitchen is very small so preparation and cooking should be done before the meeting. For sustainability reasons, we encourage everyone to bring their own place settings and utensils, including serving spoons. We have a supply of disposable plates and utensils on hand.
  • Ingredients & Allergens – The food will be cooked in home kitchens; food may contain or come into contact with common allergens. The library cannot guarantee the ingredients or preparation of any dish served at this program. We encourage everyone to bring the recipe they used noting any ingredient substitution, especially if it is a common allergen.

* Any changes to the schedule will be noted on the website calendar.

events.title: SBOOKY Library | Not-Too-Scary Halloween Fun!
events.description:
Experience the mysteries of the SBOOKY Library on Sunday, October 25, between 3 and 5 pm!

You will be invited to enter the Norman Williams Public Library’s haunted great hall in small groups and find your way along the spooky stacks. Surrounded by cobwebs and creepy noises from dark corners, you might encounter a lonely witch or hairy goblin. Beware, there may be a ghost or two!

Then it’s down, down, down – where you will discover it is nothing like a dungeon! Enjoy fun activities for all ages at the Halloween Party in the Children’s Room.

Please join us for not-too-scary tricks and treats – fun for the younger set and the less intrepid among us.

The SBOOKY LIBRARY event is free and open to all; donations to support this event are appreciated.

Adrian Tans & skeleton at a SBOOKY Library party

NOTE:

  • For everyone’s peace of mind, children under 11 must be accompanied at all times by a caregiver 14 or older.
  • The library is open from 3 to 5 pm, and there may be a line to enter. Consider staggering your arrival time.
  • Families may go through the haunted hall multiple times by exiting and rejoining the line.
  • Costumes are encouraged.

events.description:
Explore Irish Literature with a book discussion group facilitated by Karen Copenhaver and Colleen Warren at NWPL. We’ll gather on the fourth Tuesday each month, 10:30 am.

Irish literature is a rich field for discussion. From ancient mythology to modern society, Irish writers tackle urban and rural issues, political and religious divides, and the challenges and joys of life with honesty and humor.

Please come with suggestions – fiction and non-fiction, contemporary and historical. All are welcome!

events.title: Homer’s Odyssey | “One-off” Book Discussion
events.description:
Intrigued by all the buzz about the Odyssey, a poem nearly 3,000 years old? The Norman Williams Public Library will host a special “One-off” community book discussion about Homer’s ancient epic on Tuesday, October 27 at 6 pm.

Lianna Kish will guide our discussion, touching on some of its timeless themes: power, violence and the aftermath of war; wealth and poverty; marriage and family; travel, hospitality, and the yearning for home. We might explore the Bronze Age, the rich period that produced the epic, the poem’s major themes, and its lasting influence.

You are welcome to read any of the many translations of the Odyssey. The poem is available as audio editions on CD or as digital downloads. There is also a graphic novel adaptation by Garth Hines in our young adult collection.

+++

Liana Kish taught English in Newton, MA, for 24 years before moving to Vermont. She loves the slower pace of Vermont life and enjoys spending time outdoors, especially gardening and kayaking. When she’s not outside, she is often reading or trying out a new baking recipe.

events.title: Literary Pairs | Book Discussion Group
events.description:
Intrigued by how books relate to each other? A single topic can be explored from different viewpoints; a literary trope – such as retelling a classic story – can result in different endings; a shared plot might highlight divergent experiences.

Because there are two books to read for each meeting, this group usually meets quarterly on the 1st Wednesday of February, May, August, and November, at 1 pm.* Dessert will be provided!

Librarians Kathy Beaird and Lori Mitchell have teamed up to host this discussion of book pairings. Kathy has been in the book business all her adult life and loved every minute of it. Lori has been connecting readers and books for many years, including a decade here at NWPL.

Everyone is welcome! If the chosen topic or the titles pique your curiosity, please join us. Email [contact omitted] if you wish to join remotely. You can view the current theme and title selection on our Book Discussion Group page.

* Any changes to the schedule will be noted on the website calendar.

events.title: What’s On Your Nightstand? | Book Discussion Group
events.description:
This is NOT your usual Book Club! There is no assigned reading…. We chat about books you’re currently reading, books you’ve loved, and the books you’ve always wanted to read.

Along with great recommendations, our discussions have ranged from the design and appeal of book jackets, the ebook revolution, listening to audiobooks, which books we reread and why, and the craft of writing.

events.title: Emily Franklin | Love & Other Monsters
events.description:
The NWPL and Yankee Bookshop welcome Emily Franklin to talk about her newest novel, Love & Other Monsters.

In the stormy, scandalous summer of 1816, daring eighteen-year-old Claire Clairmont changed the course of literature forever. But then — unlike her stepsister Mary Shelley — she was forgotten, until now. With searing relevance to our here and now — of celebrity worship, climate disaster, of complicated femininity, Love & Other Monsters is the untold origin story of Frankenstein, a feminist reckoning of sisters, survival, and the creation of monsters — both those on the page and those who walk among us.

Emily Franklin is the bestselling author of more than twenty books, including a poetry collection, Tell Me How You Got Here. Her work has been published in The New York Times, The Boston Globe, The Kenyon Review, and The Journal of the American Medical Association, read aloud on National Public Radio, named notable by the Association of Jewish Libraries, and longlisted for the London Sunday Times Short Story Award. Her novel The Lioness of Boston, based on the life of trailblazer Isabella Stewart Gardner, is in its tenth printing.

Yankee Bookshop will be on hand with copies of Love & Other Monsters.

events.title: Veterans Day | NWPL Closed
events.description:
Veterans Day, originally known as Armistice Day, is observed annually on November 11th. It is a holiday honoring the men and women who have served in the U.S. armed forces.

The November date is important because in 1918, at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month, major hostilities of World War I formally ended when the Armistice with Germany went into effect.

events.title: Michael J. Caduto | The Day the Pond Flew South
events.description:
Award-winning writer and educator Michael J. Caduto will read his new picture book, The Day the Pond Flew South. It tells the story of Loon, who lands on a small pond from which there is no escape, though her friends try everything they can to help her fly away. As winter sets in and the pond begins to freeze, the birds invent an ingenious plan that will take every single wingbeat to save their friend.

After reading the book, the author will share a Tsimshian tale from Alaska about a loon that restores a blind man’s sight and is rewarded with the gift of its beautiful necklace. Participants may create their own “loon’s necklace” of string and beads to symbolize their relationship with this remarkable bird.

Co-hosted by Yankee Bookshop; books will be available for purchase and signing.

events.title: Poetry Group
events.description:
Writing poetry is a solitary endeavor. Are you looking for feedback on your poems? You are invited to join the Poetry Group at NWPL for sharing and critique. We meet weekly on Mondays 4 pm for about an hour and a half.*

What does it mean to critique something? According to the Oxford Dictionary, “noun: critique: a detailed analysis and assessment of something, especially a literary, philosophical, or political theory.”

Since “critique” has negative connotations, we operate in workshop format. How? Billy Collins suggested “5 Things to Consider When Analyzing Poetry in an online ‘MasterClass.’”

“Poetry involves different elements like language, rhythm, and structure. Together, they tell a story and create a complexity that is unique to poetic verse. When studying poems in-depth, look at these individual elements:

  • Theme: Poetry often conveys a message through figurative language. The central idea and the subject matter can reveal the underlying theme of a poem.
  • Language: From word choice to imagery, language creates the mood and tone of a poem. The way language is arranged also impacts the rhythm of a poem.
  • Sound and rhythm: The syllabic patterns and stresses create the metrical pattern of a poem.
  • Structure: The framework of a poem’s structure affects how it is meant to be read. A poet sculpts their story around stanzas, line breaks, rhyme patterns, punctuation, and pauses.
  • Context: The who, what, where, when, and why of a poem can help explain its purpose. Look at these elements to discover the context of a poem.”

This group is open to all; RSVP is appreciated. Please email [contact omitted].

* Any changes to the schedule will be noted on the website calendar.

events.title: Read, Cook, Eat! | Cookbook Club
events.description:
Do you like to read about cooking, experiment with recipes, share stories about food with others, and eat good food? If so, we invite you to join Read, Cook, Eat!, a cookbook discussion group. We meet at the library monthly on the 3rd Tuesday at 6 pm to share our creations.*

Newcomers are always welcome; you don’t need kitchen credentials to join! Please email [contact omitted] to register – not required but it helps us figure out how to set up the tables and chairs. And we’ll keep you updated on the books selected, or visit the Book Discussion Group page for current and past book or topic selections.

Important Details

  • Cookbooks & Recipes – We will hold a copy of the cookbook at the circulation desk for you to browse and pick out recipes you might wish to try. We’ll copy them at no charge (or you can take a photo with your phone). A second copy of the cookbook will be available to borrow for 3 days during the month leading up to the meeting.
  • Quantity & Balance – This is a true potluck affair! There may be 3 desserts and 4 vegetable dishes or an appetizer and 5 different main dishes… Since recipe yields vary widely, there is no set amount of food to bring. The goal is to discover new combinations of ingredients and flavors.
  • Equipment & Utensils – While the library has a microwave and stove for reheating, the kitchen is very small so preparation and cooking should be done before the meeting. For sustainability reasons, we encourage everyone to bring their own place settings and utensils, including serving spoons. We have a supply of disposable plates and utensils on hand.
  • Ingredients & Allergens – The food will be cooked in home kitchens; food may contain or come into contact with common allergens. The library cannot guarantee the ingredients or preparation of any dish served at this program. We encourage everyone to bring the recipe they used noting any ingredient substitution, especially if it is a common allergen.

* Any changes to the schedule will be noted on the website calendar.

events.title: Ethan Tapper | The Forest Year: Finding Hope in a World Worth Saving
events.description:
Ethan Tapper knows what it means to care for a forest ecosystem. In The Forest Year: Finding Hope in a World Worth Saving, he explores the practices of staying, caretaking, and paying attention.

The Yankee Bookshop and Norman Williams Public Library are excited to welcome the author back to Woodstock with his stunning follow-up to the award-winning How to Love a Forest: The Bittersweet Work of Tending a Changing World. Both place-based and practice-driven, Tapper writes not as an armchair philosopher or an academic, but as a working forester and ecologist stewarding real forests in real time, blending emotional insight with ecological rigor.

With lyrical meditations across all four seasons, we experience the beautiful interconnectedness of flowers, birds, fungi, and trees, and come to see how each is part of a living, breathing whole. Grounded in close observation and a deep sense of place, Ethan shows how tending the land is also a way of tending ourselves. At a time of uncertainty, The Forest Year offers a gentle, sustaining vision: that by becoming rooted—by noticing, returning, and caring—we can find both meaning and resilience in the natural world.

+++

Ethan Tapper is a forester, ecologist, digital storyteller, and author. For more than a decade, Ethan has been recognized as a thought-leader in the world of ecosystem stewardship, winning numerous regional and national awards for his work. He works, writes, hunts, birds, and runs a small consulting forestry business from his home at Bear Island—his 175-acre working forest, homestead, orchard, and sugarbush in Vermont—and plays in a punk band.

+++

“So much humility and wonder shines through Tapper’s prose…a well-earned, luminous, and ever-more-precious tribute to this northern forest.” — Helen Whybrow, author of The Salt Stones

Don’t hesitate to get in touch with the Children’s librarians for more information or to sign up.

“Chess helps you to concentrate, improve your logic. It teaches you to play by the rules and take responsibility for your actions, how to problem solve in an uncertain environment.” – Garry Kasparov

events.title: Toddler Story Time
events.description:
Enjoy stories, socializing, and often a project tied to the theme of the books we read.

Geared toward young children aged 20 months to 3½ years, we gather for 30 minutes to an hour, depending on attention spans.

Information on our other scheduled Story Times can be found on the Children’s pages.

Any changes to the schedule for holidays will be noted on the website calendar. Please email [contact omitted] for more information.

events.title: Enchanted Wassail Evening
events.description:
We invite you to begin the special weekend at our Enchanted Wassail Evening! Embrace the holiday spirit, support the Library, and join us for a community celebration of the season.

Join your neighbors and friends for complimentary drinks and delectable hor d’oeuvres, while enjoying the refreshing sounds of The Preacher and the Teacher, an indie duo featuring Rev. Leon Dunkley and Stephen Stuntz.

The Library is a vital part of the vibrant Woodstock community and relies on your support to offer an array of programs and services free of charge to all.

Tickets are $75. You have several options to purchase tickets:

    • Stop by the library to pay with cash, check, credit card, or Venmo.
    • Mail a check to NWPL “Enchanted Wassail Evening,” 10 The Green, Woodstock, VT 05091.
    • Send payment via Venmo: nwpl-library (be sure to note how many tickets you are purchasing)
    • To pay online CLICK HERE.

Lights twinkle, greenery scents the air, and music fills the elegant historic building. We hope you will join us!

+++

Sponsorship opportunities for this special holiday fundraising event are available. Please be sure to mention “Wassail” with your donation.

Please email [contact omitted] with any questions.

events.title: Rare & Vintage Book Sale
events.description:
Just in time for the holidays, Norman Williams Public Library is offering an intriguing collection of rare and vintage books—in addition to the ongoing book sale in the foyer.

From signed, century-old gems to rare classics, illustrated children’s books to ornate, pocket-sized poetry collections, we invite you to stop by and discover a special book to treasure.

Come Friday for the best selection (and easiest parking) or stop by on Saturday in between the myriad of other activities in the library and around town.

Proceeds fund new books for the adult and youth collections, support programs and events, and help maintain our historic library building.

events.title: Stories of the Season for Children
events.description:
Join us for a lively reading of storybooks celebrating winter and the holiday season. We’ll gather after school and begin the readings and related activities at 3:30 pm, after everyone has had a little snack and gotten settled.

December brings the Winter Solstice, Hanukkah, Christmas, and more! These short, dark days are marked with a variety of different traditions. Animals also have ways of adapting to the cold and snow.

We invite you to gather family and friends for an hour of fun and festive tales.

Free and open to the public.

Illustrations projected on the big screen!

Please note: Children 10 and younger must be accompanied at all times by a caregiver 14 or older.:

events.title: Family Story Time
events.description:
Grandparents, parents, and caregivers are invited to bring their young charges to enjoy stories. We’ll select picture books about the season, or a theme, or perhaps feature new additions to our collection.

Everyone is welcome on Saturday mornings at 10:30. Discover new picture books or savor old favorites with the younger family members.

events.title: Ham Gillett presents Dylan Thomas’s Lyrical Portrait of Holidays Past
events.description:
Send the kids outside to romp, take off your apron, stash the light-hanging ladder, and join us on Saturday, December 12, from 12:00-12:30 OR 1:00-1:30 for Ham Gillett’s traditional Wassail reading.

The Welsh poet Dylan Thomas looks back with a child’s-eye view of a magical time of presents, family, and newly fallen snow in the seasonal classic A Child’s Christmas in Wales, written in the early 1950s.

Ham Gillett has shared this story during Wassail Weekend for more years than he can remember. He offers us a time to be still, to close our eyes, and be transported by Thomas’s matchless weaving of lyrical words and evocative images.

The Uncles (from A Child’s Christmas in Wales) Illustration by Fritz Eichenberg

“Our snow … came shawling out of the ground and swam and drifted out of the arms and hands and bodies of the trees; snow grew overnight on the roofs of the houses like a pure and grandfather moss, minutely-ivied the walls and settled on the postman, opening the gate, like a dumb, numb thunder-storm of white, torn Christmas cards.” – Dylan Thomas

+++

This reading is free and open to the public and – despite the essay’s title – is geared toward listeners 10 and older. First-come, first-seated; space is limited.

events.title: “Let All the Nations Sing!” | A Wrensong Holiday Concert
events.description:
Wrensong presents a festive concert of a cappella choral music celebrating Christmas and the winter season.

This year, they are bringing you songs from around the world, including rarely heard Renaissance works from Italian composer Pomponio Nenna and Guatemalan composer Tomás Pascual, contemporary pieces from Kenya and Nigeria, and cherished American classics. The program also includes glorious songs from Sweden, France, Spain, and Peru, all sung in their original languages.

Wrensong is an a cappella choral group from Vermont’s Upper Valley that focuses on the vocal treasures of the Renaissance. Their repertoire ranges from the secular to the religious, and concerts often include narration aimed at giving audiences a context for listening with understanding.

Join us for this uplifting concert of holiday music as we welcome the season in international style. Free and open to the public. Seating is limited; first-come, first-seated.

events.title: Poetry Group
events.description:
Writing poetry is a solitary endeavor. Are you looking for feedback on your poems? You are invited to join the Poetry Group at NWPL for sharing and critique. We meet weekly on Mondays 4 pm for about an hour and a half.*

What does it mean to critique something? According to the Oxford Dictionary, “noun: critique: a detailed analysis and assessment of something, especially a literary, philosophical, or political theory.”

Since “critique” has negative connotations, we operate in workshop format. How? Billy Collins suggested “5 Things to Consider When Analyzing Poetry in an online ‘MasterClass.’”

“Poetry involves different elements like language, rhythm, and structure. Together, they tell a story and create a complexity that is unique to poetic verse. When studying poems in-depth, look at these individual elements:

  • Theme: Poetry often conveys a message through figurative language. The central idea and the subject matter can reveal the underlying theme of a poem.
  • Language: From word choice to imagery, language creates the mood and tone of a poem. The way language is arranged also impacts the rhythm of a poem.
  • Sound and rhythm: The syllabic patterns and stresses create the metrical pattern of a poem.
  • Structure: The framework of a poem’s structure affects how it is meant to be read. A poet sculpts their story around stanzas, line breaks, rhyme patterns, punctuation, and pauses.
  • Context: The who, what, where, when, and why of a poem can help explain its purpose. Look at these elements to discover the context of a poem.”

This group is open to all; RSVP is appreciated. Please email [contact omitted].

* Any changes to the schedule will be noted on the website calendar.
